          Michael Carrick's Stay of Execution? Four Big Questions Facing Man Utd Over Next Nine Days
        
      
                          
                      Oct 30, 2026
          
                      Ryan Benson / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
When all seemed lost for Michael Carrick, Manchester United opted against dismissing him. But are they actually just biding their time ahead of the international break?

In the same week, Manchester United were battered by Como and Bournemouth, while the captain – who was dropped for the latter game – appeared to publicly criticise the coaching staff’s tactics. Somehow, Michael Carrick survived this.

The pressure was already on Carrick following a dismal start to the season, and there seemed to be no way out for him after the loss to Bournemouth at Old Trafford. But the United hierarchy opted to stay their blade; Carrick avoided the axe for the time being.

It’s plausible the vociferous backing of Carrick from fans at Old Trafford – and the intense fury directed specifically at the players and club decision-makers – persuaded the club to give him more time. But with the next international break just around the corner and such moments typically seen as opportune times to change managers, Carrick is by no means out of the woods.

Whether the club actually want to give him more time or if this is just a stay of execution, only time will tell. But the overriding sense is that Carrick has a maximum of three games to save his job.
These are the key questions facing United over the next week or so…

Given how disappointing United’s performances have been, particularly against Como and Bournemouth, it’s difficult to see a way out for Carrick right now. They were so comfortably beaten in both games that the upturn in performance level needs to be incredibly dramatic and swift for him to save himself.
Obviously Carrick has managed to get a tune out of United before; their 39 points won last season after his appointment was more than any other club.

But the atmosphere clearly isn’t great, confidence is shot, and the situation with Bruno Fernandes going rogue during/after the Como game hardly gives the impression that the players are fully behind Carrick.
United’s outlook also isn’t helped by having a difficult run coming up before the international break.

In the Opta Power Rankings, their three upcoming opponents in all competitions (Chelsea, Roma, Villa) have an average rating of 93.2 out of 100; only three Premier League clubs have tougher opposition before the international break. And of the nine English clubs competing in Europe, all facing three matches in the next nine days, none have a tougher schedule than Manchester United.
If Carrick can get them back on track in the next 10 days, it will be genuinely impressive.

Match context has played a part, but it appears there’s been an attempt from United to have more control this season, straying slightly from the style that seemingly suited them so well under Carrick last term.

Possession is up from 49% to 56%, and they’re averaging an extra 43 final-third passes per game compared to the second half of 2025-26. So, that gives you an idea that they’re having more territory. Not that it's done them much good.

They have had more shots than anyone else, though the average xG value of those attempts is just 0.08, the second worst after Tottenham (0.07). And when they do create clear opportunities, they’ve not been clinical enough; only three teams are underperforming in relation to their xG to a greater degree than United (-2.8) this season.
The outlook in attack is pretty bleak, then, and it’s not much better at the other end.
Their opponents’ average xG per shot of 0.14 against United is the highest in the division, and their 40.2% of shots faced landing on target is the second-highest.
So, even though they aren’t conceding that many shots, the chances they are giving up are of high-quality.

There are numerous potential causes for this, and it’s fair to suggest their backline and midfield being so disrupted won’t have helped. But there’s an argument they could have done more to help themselves.

For instance, instead of moving for a greater degree of control, they might have decided that collectively sitting deeper to prioritise being compact and protecting their own goal while looking for transition opportunities was the best course of action.
